title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: a single blade of grass that fire cannot burn and wind cannot lift

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wave of beauty: without Shakti, Shiva cannot even stir.

The gods have just won a victory, and they're very pleased with themselves. So begins a short scene in the Kena Upanishad. Then something appears that they don't recognize: a mysterious being, a yaksha. Agni, the fire, goes up to it, boasting that he can burn anything on earth. The being sets down one blade of grass and says: burn this. Agni throws everything he has at it. The grass doesn't even scorch. Then Vayu, the wind, who says he can carry off anything at all. He can't lift it an inch. Two gods, two powers, one straw.
screen: `THE GODS ARE PROUD.` → `ONE BLADE OF GRASS.` → `FIRE CAN'T BURN IT. WIND CAN'T LIFT IT.`

segments.voice: Next the gods send Indra, their king. He walks toward the being, and it vanishes. In that same space he meets a woman, radiant and beautifully adorned: Uma, the daughter of the Himalaya. What was that? he asks. She tells him. That was Brahman, the ultimate reality. Your victory was its victory, and you took the credit. First, the lesson about power. Fire could burn and wind could blow because something greater let them. Take that away, and even a blade of grass is too heavy. The gods' powers were real, but borrowed. Second, who explains it. The one who can name Brahman to the king of the gods is Uma, a woman of the mountains. Later tradition knows Uma as a name of Parvati, Shiva's wife. Some who worship the goddess point to this scene: when the gods are lost, Shakti is the teacher who stands in the empty place and speaks. Third, where she appears: in the very space where the being vanished. Some readers hear the heart of the idea there. Brahman is beyond sight, beyond fire and wind; Shakti is the side of that reality that turns toward you, the face that answers. Fourth, the plainest. The scene begins with pride and ends with a question. Indra doesn't win anything here. He just asks, and listens. The Upanishad says Agni, Vayu and Indra came to stand above the other gods because they came closest to Brahman, and Indra above them because he was the first to know it.
screen: `THE BEING VANISHES. UMA IS THERE.` · `THE GODS' POWERS WERE BORROWED.` · `UMA IS THE ONE WHO KNOWS.` · `SHE STANDS IN THE EMPTY PLACE.` · then, large: `THAT WAS BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Watch for the moment a thought ends: a plan finishes, a memory fades, a sound outside stops. Don't rush to the next one; stay in that small empty place for a breath or two, the way Indra stayed where the being disappeared. If you pray, you can hold the name of the goddess, or the name you use for God, in that empty place. If you don't, just keep waiting there.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Kena Upanishad, fire and wind fail before one blade of grass, and Uma stands where the mystery vanished and names it Brahman.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Even fire and wind were running on borrowed power. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Kena Upanishad is studied in Vedanta schools, and the scene of Uma explaining Brahman to Indra is retold in talks on the goddess.

chat.says: In that Kena story, why couldn't the fire god burn one blade of grass?
options: His power was borrowed: Brahman let fire burn, and without it even grass was too much.
The grass was soaked from a storm, so even the fire god couldn't get it to light.
Agni was worn out from the battle and had used up all of his own fire already.
chat.meaning: Uma tells Indra the being was Brahman: the gods' victory was its victory. Fire and wind could act only by that greater power.
